title: Ahead-of-Time Compilation & Native Images
summary: Compiling a managed-language program fully to native code before it ever runs — trading the JIT's runtime flexibility and profile-guided optimization for instant startup and a small footprint, the opposite end of the spectrum from just-in-time-compilation.

slides.markdown:
`just-in-time-compilation` opened with a spectrum: pure interpretation → JIT → ahead-of-time (AOT). This topic is the far end of that spectrum, taken seriously.

**AOT compilation** compiles a managed-language program fully to native machine code *before it ships*, the same way a C or Rust compiler does. No JIT, no warm-up, often no separate runtime step at all. The payoff is startup speed and a small footprint; the cost is giving up the JIT's biggest advantage — optimizing based on what the program actually does at runtime — and, for languages built around dynamic features, giving up some of those features too.

This is the direct fix for the cold-start problem `what-a-runtime-provides` and `just-in-time-compilation` both raised, and it's exactly why serverless and CLI tooling increasingly reach for it.

Three concrete wins AOT offers over a JIT'd runtime:

- **No JIT warm-up.** The native code you ship is the fastest code that program will ever run — there's no interpreted-then-C1-then-C2 ramp, because there's no JIT at all.
- **Smaller footprint.** No JIT compiler threads, no bytecode-to-be-compiled sitting around, often a smaller memory footprint overall since a build-time compiler can strip unreachable code (dead-code elimination across the *whole* program, not just one method).
- **Faster, more predictable cold start.** A GraalVM native-image binary commonly starts in single-digit to tens of milliseconds, versus a JVM's hundreds — this is the number that makes AOT worth discussing for serverless functions specifically.

At a cost: none of this is free, which the rest of this topic makes concrete.

slides.subTitle: Reflection and dynamic class loading
slides.markdown:
AOT compilation needs to know, at build time, what code might ever run — because it's compiling everything ahead of the fact. Anything a program decides at *runtime* (loading a class by name from a string, generating a proxy class dynamically, calling a method resolved via reflection) breaks that assumption unless the AOT compiler is told about it in advance.

GraalVM native-image handles this with **configuration files** listing every reflectively-accessed class/method up front, generated by a build-time agent that traces a representative run of your program. Miss one, and the reflective call fails at runtime with no fallback — there's no JIT sitting there ready to compile the missed case on demand. This is a real migration cost for existing codebases built around heavy reflection (many dependency-injection frameworks, some ORMs).

slides.sectionTitle: GraalVM native-image and the closed-world assumption
slides.markdown:
GraalVM's native-image tool builds on what it calls the **closed-world assumption**: at build time, it must be able to see the entire reachable call graph of the program — every class that might get loaded, every method that might get called — because anything outside that graph simply won't exist in the final binary.

This is a meaningfully stronger requirement than a normal JVM's classpath, where classes can be loaded dynamically at any point with no advance warning. The practical implication: dynamic class loading, unrestricted reflection, and JVM bytecode manipulation libraries (common in older dependency-injection and mocking frameworks) either need to be avoided, explicitly declared via config, or replaced with build-time equivalents that don't rely on runtime surprises — several major Java frameworks (Spring, Micronaut, Quarkus) have shipped native-image-specific modes specifically to satisfy this.

slides.sectionTitle: Go and Rust: statically compiled by default
slides.markdown:
Go and Rust aren't retrofitting AOT onto a managed-runtime model — they were designed around it from the start, and ship native binaries with no separate runtime step comparable to a JVM or CLR at all.

That said, "no runtime" is a simplification worth being precise about in an interview: Go embeds a scheduler and garbage collector directly into every compiled binary (there's no external Go "VM," but there is runtime *code*, statically linked in), and Rust's ownership/borrow-checking (`ownership-and-borrowing`, `memory-gc` group) happens entirely at compile time, so a compiled Rust binary has essentially no runtime memory-management code running at all beyond what you wrote. Both are meaningfully different from "AOT-compiled Java," which still carries a GC and other JVM-derived runtime services inside the native image.

slides.sectionTitle: JIT vs AOT, head to head
slides.markdown:
| | JIT | AOT (native-image / Native AOT / Go / Rust) |
|---|---|---|
| Startup | Slow (warm-up) | Fast (native code from instruction one) |
| Peak throughput | Best — profile-guided, adapts to real behavior | Good, but fixed at build time — no runtime adaptation |
| Reflection/dynamic loading | Fully supported | Restricted or must be declared ahead of time |
| Best fit | Long-running server processes | Serverless, CLI tools, containers that scale to zero |

Neither wins universally — a service handling millions of requests over hours benefits from the JIT's ability to specialize for its *actual* traffic pattern; a function invoked once every few minutes never lives long enough for that specialization to pay off, and pays the warm-up cost on every cold invocation instead.

slides.sectionTitle: "AOT is strictly better" is the pitfall
slides.markdown:
Given AOT's fast, predictable startup, it's tempting to treat it as a strict upgrade over JIT — faster start, why wouldn't you always want that?

The honest cost: AOT compiles once, with whatever information is available at build time, and never again. A JIT compiler, given the same code running for hours, will eventually out-optimize the AOT version on the specific inputs and code paths that program actually hits in production — inlining decisions, speculative devirtualization, and inline caches all improve *because* the JIT watched real behavior, something no build-time compiler can do.

This is exactly the crossover-point pattern from complexity analysis: AOT wins on short-lived, cold-start-dominated workloads; JIT wins once a process runs long enough for adaptive optimization to pay for its own warm-up cost. Treating one as universally superior is the mistake — the right answer depends on how long the process lives.

A GraalVM native-image build looks close to a normal Java build with one extra, expensive step:

```bash
# Trace a representative run to generate reflection/resource config
java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=config/ -jar app.jar

# Build the native binary using that config, doing whole-program
# reachability analysis (this step can take minutes, not seconds)
native-image --class-path app.jar -H:ConfigurationFileDirectories=config/ -o app

# Runs like any native binary, no JVM, no JIT, no classloading step
./app
```

The build step is the price paid up front so every subsequent `./app` invocation skips everything `the-jvm-deep-dive` described as cold-start cost — it's a genuine shift of cost from every runtime invocation to a single build.

A serverless function's economics are the AOT case study: it may run for milliseconds, get billed by execution time, and — worst case — cold-start on every single invocation if traffic is sparse enough that the platform doesn't keep an instance warm.

Under that model, a JVM's 100–300ms of classloading and interpreted warm-up isn't a one-time cost amortized over a long process lifetime — it's paid, in the worst case, on every invocation, and it's pure overhead the caller waits on and pays for. A native-image binary starting in single-digit milliseconds turns that overhead into a rounding error, which is precisely why AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, and similar platforms have invested specifically in GraalVM native-image and Native AOT support rather than just "a faster JVM."

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a serverless function's benefit, precisely
slides.markdown:
A complete answer to "why would a serverless function benefit from a native image over a JIT'd runtime" names the mechanism, not just the conclusion:

1. **The workload shape** — short-lived, frequently cold-started, billed per invocation — never gives a JIT enough sustained execution to amortize its warm-up or reach its optimized tiers.
2. **The specific cost being avoided** — classloading, interpreted execution, and multi-tier JIT ramp-up, all paid before the function's actual logic even starts.
3. **The trade accepted in exchange** — reduced dynamic-reflection support, and no runtime adaptation to traffic patterns the way a long-lived JIT'd service would get.

That third point is the one candidates skip, and skipping it is what separates a fresher's "AOT is faster" answer from a senior's "AOT is faster because this workload never earns back a JIT's investment."
